office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The Hanover Community School Corporation is based at 14525 Wicker Ave. in Cedar Lake [24]. Its board races appear on ballots in Cedar Lake, in Hanover Township and in some St. John precincts [25, 26, 27]. It runs Jane Ball, Lincoln and Red Cedars elementary schools, Hanover Central Middle School and Hanover Central High School [28]. Federal (NCES) data compiled by Plain Schools show 2,831 students in 2024–25 [29].

Superintendent (2026): Dr. Mary Tracy-MacAulay led the June 16, 2026 meeting, where board members thanked her as she left the district [30]. By July 21, 2026, Phil Misecko, the former assistant superintendent, was superintendent and described the transition as 'a learning curve' [31, 32]. Dr. John Zack became assistant superintendent of curriculum and instruction in July 2026 [33]. The county's Aug. 13, 2026 officials directory still lists Tracy-MacAulay [34].

The board has five members: one elected at large and two from each of Districts 1 and 2 [34]. The current members are President Tracy Haskell (at large), Vice President Scott Burdan (District 2), Secretary Aaron Kuzma (District 2), Tara Beilke (District 1) and Eric Valiska (District 1) [24, 34]. Voters across the district vote in both district races: sample ballots for Cedar Lake, Hanover Township and St. John precincts all list District 1 and District 2 [25, 26, 27].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: one District 1 seat and one District 2 seat, each 'Vote For One (1) Only,' which matches the state list [25]. Valiska holds the District 1 seat and Kuzma the District 2 seat, and both terms end Dec. 31, 2026 [34]. Both are running for reelection, each against one challenger [35].

Past results: in 2022 Valiska won District 1 with 1,834 votes, 31 more than Constance Sterkowitz (1,803), with Nichole Lebeter third (1,126). Kuzma won District 2 with 1,791 votes, ahead of Jeffrey Majewski (1,496) and three others [36]. Haskell (at large), Beilke (District 1) and Burdan (District 2) won in 2024, and their terms run through 2028 [37, 34].

Operating referendum renewal (2025): on Nov. 4, 2025 voters approved renewing the district's operating referendum, 1,690 to 1,516 (52.71%) [38]. The renewal lasts eight years at a maximum rate of $0.29 and was projected to raise about $5.16 million a year. The planned uses are managing class sizes ($2.51 million), transportation ($1.48 million), student safety and security ($760,000) and teacher retention ($410,000). The levy was first approved in 2015 and extended in 2020 [39].

Bonds and 2027 budget (fall 2026): the board scheduled hearings for Sept. 8 and Oct. 13, 2026 on a preliminary determination to issue general obligation bonds. The bonds would pay for districtwide HVAC, boiler and chiller work, paving, flooring, building and athletic facility improvements, and buses [40]. A related additional appropriation of $3,605,000 was set for the Oct. 13 hearing [41]. The Oct. 13 agenda also includes the public hearing on the 2027 budget, levies and tax rates, the 2027–2029 capital projects plan and the 2027–2031 bus replacement plan [28]. This guide found no district statement on the effect of the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1).

Cell phones and discipline (June 2026): on June 16, 2026 the board voted 5–0 to adopt a replacement personal communication devices policy (5136). The minutes say the district 'took the lesser of the two options to make it easier on our children and their families.' Haskell said phones need to be allowed at school, especially for extracurricular activities, and Burdan said the matter was 'out of our control.' The board also revised its student discipline, suspension and expulsion, and search and seizure policies [30].

Other 2026 actions: in July 2026 the board approved a school resource officer agreement for 2026–27, the classified staff salary schedule and 2026–27 student fees. All votes were 3–0, with Beilke and Valiska not listed as present [31].
Forums: this guide found no candidate forums, questionnaires or news coverage of the 2026 Hanover school board races.

candidates.summary: Incumbent; a social studies teacher at T.F. South High School, first elected in 2022 [24, 36].
background: Has taught social studies at T.F. South High School since 2000 [24]. Holds a bachelor's degree in history and secondary education from Illinois Wesleyan University and a master's degree in curriculum and instruction [24]. Has lived in Cedar Lake since 2009 [24].
Serves as the board's liaison to the St. John Redevelopment Commission and the St. John Park Board [28].
path_to_ballot: Filed May 20, 2026 as a Republican, and 'Republican Party' is printed under his name on the ballot [35, 25, 6]. In 2022 he was listed as nonpartisan and won the seat by 31 votes [36].
on_incumbent: Is a current board member. At the June 16, 2026 meeting he moved to accept a set of donations and seconded approval of summer pay rates for certified staff; both passed 5–0 [30]. He also said how much Tracy-MacAulay cared about everyone [30].
gaps: No campaign statements, website, questionnaire responses, endorsements or finance reports found.
No stated positions on the bond projects, the 2027 budget or SEA 1 found.

candidates.summary: Challenger for the District 1 seat; not a current board member [35, 24].
path_to_ballot: Filed June 18, 2026 as nonpartisan; 'Non-Partisan' is printed under his name on the ballot [35, 25, 6].
gaps: No news coverage, campaign statements, website, questionnaire responses, endorsements or finance reports found.
Occupation and ties to the schools not found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board secretary; a union electrician foreman and registered nurse, first elected in 2022 [24, 36].
background: Works as a foreman electrician with IBEW Local 701 in the Chicago area after completing its five-year apprenticeship [24]. Holds an associate degree in nursing from Purdue University and is a licensed registered nurse [24]. Is a U.S. Army infantry veteran and a 1992 graduate of Lake Central High School [24]. Has lived in the Hanover community since 2011 [24].
Serves as the board's liaison to the St. John Town Council [28].
path_to_ballot: Filed June 4, 2026 as a Republican, and 'Republican Party' is printed under his name on the ballot [35, 25, 6]. In 2022 he was listed as nonpartisan and won District 2 with 35.09% in a five-way race [36].
on_incumbent: Is a current board member and serves as secretary [24]. In July 2026 he moved to approve the consent agenda and an overnight basketball camp, and both passed 3–0 [31]. In June 2026 he thanked Tracy-MacAulay for her 'guidance and mentorship' [30].
gaps: No campaign statements, website, questionnaire responses, endorsements or finance reports found.
No stated positions on the bond projects, the 2027 budget or SEA 1 found.

candidates.summary: Challenger for the District 2 seat; not a current board member [35, 24].
path_to_ballot: Filed June 16, 2026 as a Republican, and 'Republican Party' is printed under his name on the ballot [35, 25, 6].

County results list a Jeffrey Majewski who finished second in the 2022 District 2 race with 1,496 votes, and a Jeffrey Dale Majewski who lost the 2024 District 2 race to Scott Burdan, 4,451 to 3,953 [36, 37]. The name and seat match, but this guide did not confirm that these are the same person.
gaps: No news coverage, campaign statements, website, questionnaire responses, endorsements or finance reports found.
Occupation and ties to the schools not found.
